pages.x: By 1899 foreign powers had carved China into spheres of influence, and missionaries, railways and foreign goods angered many in the north, where floods and drought had brought hunger. A secret society that foreigners called the Boxers, for their martial arts, spread through Shandong, killing missionaries and Chinese Christians. Its members believed their rituals made them proof against bullets.

Empress Dowager Cixi, who had ruled China from behind the throne for nearly 40 years, at first wavered. In June 1900, as Boxers poured into Beijing and foreign troops seized the forts guarding the sea road to it, she sided with the Boxers and declared war on all the foreign powers at once.

For 55 days some 900 foreigners and about 3,000 Chinese Christians held out in the legation quarter of Beijing, where the foreign embassies stood, behind barricades of sandbags and furniture. The German envoy was shot dead in the street. Boxers and imperial troops attacked again and again, but never with their full strength.

In the northern countryside Boxers killed tens of thousands of Chinese Christians, and some 200 foreign missionaries and their children. When the foreign armies came, they took a terrible revenge, burning villages and killing far more Chinese, Boxers or not.
pages.of: Chinese Christians killed by the Boxers

pages.x: An army of eight nations, Japan, Russia, Britain, France, the United States, Germany, Italy and Austria-Hungary, fought its way from Tianjin and broke into Beijing on 14 August, ending the siege. Cixi fled the city dressed as a peasant woman, and foreign soldiers looted the capital for weeks.

In 1901 China signed the Boxer Protocol. It had to execute officials who had backed the Boxers, let foreign troops guard the embassies and pay 450 million ounces of silver over 39 years. The United States later used part of its share to send Chinese students to America and to found Tsinghua University in Beijing.

The rising was a disaster for the Qing. Humbled again, the court at last tried real reforms, ending the old exams in 1905, but too late: the dynasty fell ten years after the protocol. Chinese remember the Boxers both as a cruel, backward rising and as a cry of resistance to foreign bullying.
